blocks.html: Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios (recall §5.5.1–5.5.3) judge a test at one chosen cut-off. Many tests give a continuous reading (MUAC, haemoglobin, a risk score), and the cut-off is a choice. §15.5.1 shows how a test performs over every possible cut-off at once and how to pick one. §15.5.2 applies the same tools to the predicted probabilities of a regression model and adds the checks a prediction model needs.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots a test’s sensitivity against (1 − specificity) at every possible cut-off. The area under the curve (AUC) is the probability that a randomly chosen person with the disease has a more abnormal test value than a randomly chosen person without it. It runs from 0 to 1: 0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect separation, and a value below 0.5 means the test works in the opposite direction to the one specified.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Each cut-off gives one pair of sensitivity and specificity (recall §5.5.1), so each cut-off is one point on the curve. A very lenient cut-off calls almost everyone positive: sensitivity near 1, specificity near 0, the top-right corner. A very strict cut-off does the reverse, the bottom-left corner. A test that separates the groups perfectly climbs straight up the left edge to sensitivity 1 before moving right. A useless test runs along the diagonal, where sensitivity equals the false-positive proportion at every cut-off.

The AUC compresses the curve into one number. It does not depend on any cut-off, so it is the natural way to compare candidate tests before a cut-off is chosen.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why is the area a probability? Take n₁ diseased and n₀ non-diseased people. Step the cut-off down one value at a time. Each time the cut-off passes a diseased person, the curve rises by 1/n₁. Each time it passes a non-diseased person, it moves right by 1/n₀. The area added by one step to the right equals its width, 1/n₀, times the current height, which is the proportion of diseased people already passed, that is, with a more abnormal value than this non-diseased person. Adding over all non-diseased people:

AUC = (number of diseased–non-diseased pairs in which the diseased person is more abnormal) ÷ (n₁ × n₀),

with tied pairs counted as one-half. This count is the Mann–Whitney U of §10.2 (recall: U counts the pairs in which one group’s member has the larger value), so AUC = U/(n₁n₀) (Hanley & McNeil, 1982). If the direction is specified the wrong way round, every “win” becomes a “loss” and the AUC becomes 1 − AUC, hence values below 0.5.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Mid-upper-arm circumference (MUAC) is quick to measure in an anganwadi. Suppose (hypothetical data) 20 children aged 6–59 months also have their weight-for-height measured, and 10 of them have severe acute malnutrition (SAM) by that reference standard. Low MUAC means “positive”.

MUAC (cm)
SAM (n = 10) 10.8, 11.2, 11.4, 11.6, 11.9, 12.0, 12.3, 12.6, 12.9, 13.4
Not SAM (n = 10) 11.8, 12.4, 12.7, 13.0, 13.2, 13.5, 13.7, 14.0, 14.3, 14.8

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Pairs: 10 × 10 = 100. Count the pairs in which the SAM child has the lower MUAC. For each non-SAM child, count the SAM children below it: 11.8 cm has 4 below it (10.8, 11.2, 11.4, 11.6); 12.4 has 7; 12.7 has 8; 13.0 and 13.2 have 9 each; the five from 13.5 upwards have 10 each. Total 4 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 9 + 50 = 87, no ties.
  2. AUC = 87/100 = 0.87.
  3. One cut-off: “positive if MUAC ≤ 12.6 cm”. Sensitivity = 8/10 = 0.8 (SAM children at or below 12.6). Specificity = 8/10 = 0.8 (non-SAM children above 12.6: all but 11.8 and 12.4). The point is (0.2, 0.8).
  4. Youden’s J = Se + Sp − 1 (recall §5.5.3) at each cut-off. It peaks at 0.6 at three cut-offs: ≤ 12.3 cm (Se 0.7, Sp 0.9), ≤ 12.6 cm (0.8, 0.8) and ≤ 12.9 cm (0.9, 0.7).
  5. J cannot choose among them, because J weights a missed case and a false alarm equally. A missed SAM child can die; a false positive costs a referral visit. A screening programme would take ≤ 12.9 cm (Se 0.9). A programme with scarce referral places might take ≤ 12.3 cm (Sp 0.9, LR+ = 0.7/0.1 = 7.0).

blocks.alt: ROC curve for the MUAC example
blocks.caption: Figure 15.7. ROC curve for MUAC as a screen for SAM (hypothetical 10 vs 10 children). Each step is one cut-off. The three orange points share the maximum Youden J of 0.6. AUC = 0.87.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(pROC)
# first 10 SAM, last 10 not SAM
muac <- c(10.8, 11.2, 11.4, 11.6, 11.9, 12.0, 12.3, 12.6, 12.9, 13.4,
          11.8, 12.4, 12.7, 13.0, 13.2, 13.5, 13.7, 14.0, 14.3, 14.8)
sam  <- rep(1:0, each = 10)
# low MUAC = positive
r <- roc(sam, muac, direction = ">", levels = c(0, 1))
auc(r); ci.auc(r)
coords(r, "best", best.method = "youden")
# direction reversed
auc(roc(sam, muac, direction = "<", levels = c(0, 1)))
Area under the curve: 0.87
95% CI: 0.7124-1 (DeLong)
  threshold specificity sensitivity
1     12.95         0.7         0.9
2     12.65         0.8         0.8
3     12.35         0.9         0.7
Area under the curve: 0.13

direction = ">" tells roc that the non-SAM group has the higher values. The AUC of 0.87 is step 2. Its DeLong 95% CI runs from 0.71 to 1 (the upper limit is cut at 1): with only 20 children, the AUC is imprecise. coords returns the three tied Youden cut-offs of step 4; pROC reports each threshold as the midpoint between two observed values (12.95 lies between 12.9 and 13.0). The last line specifies the direction wrongly and gets 1 − 0.87 = 0.13.

points.html: AUC runs from 0 to 1. 0.5 is chance. Below 0.5 the test is informative but the “positive” direction was specified the wrong way round; reversing it gives 1 − AUC.

Rough labels are a convention. An often-quoted scale, from Hosmer and Lemeshow’s logistic regression textbook, calls 0.7–0.8 “acceptable”, 0.8–0.9 “excellent” and above 0.9 “outstanding” (Mandrekar, 2010). Whether an AUC is good enough depends on the use: a triage score at 0.75 may help; a confirmatory test at 0.85 may not.

The curve does not choose the cut-off. Youden’s J is one rule, and it assumes equal costs of the two errors. The clinical cost of a false negative against a false positive, and the prevalence where the test will be used (recall §5.5.2), should decide.
Once a cut-off is chosen, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios at that cut-off are computed as in §5.5.1–5.5.3. Report their CIs (recall §7.2.4) and the AUC’s CI.
Two tests with the same AUC can differ where it matters. One curve may be higher at the high-sensitivity end, which is the end a screening programme uses.
The reference standard must be independent of the test. If the test result helps define “diseased”, sensitivity and the AUC are inflated.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.8

questions.prompt: An ROC curve for a new biomarker lies almost on the diagonal. A second analyst reports an AUC of 0.21 for another marker. What does each result mean, and what should the second analyst check first?
questions.answer: The diagonal is where sensitivity equals the false-positive proportion (1 − specificity) at every cut-off: the test is no better than chance, AUC ≈ 0.5. An AUC of 0.21 is far from chance: the marker separates the groups well, but in the opposite direction to the one specified. The analyst should first check the direction (for example, whether low values indicate disease, as with MUAC). Reversing it gives AUC = 1 − 0.21 = 0.79.

questions.prompt: A study has 8 diseased and 5 non-diseased people. Of the 40 diseased–non-diseased pairs, the diseased person has the higher biomarker value in 30, the values are tied in 4, and the non-diseased person is higher in 6. Compute the AUC.
questions.answer: AUC = (pairs won + ½ × ties) ÷ all pairs = (30 + ½ × 4) ÷ 40 = 32/40 = 0.80. (Check: 30 + 4 + 6 = 40 = 8 × 5.)

questions.prompt: In the MUAC example, compute Youden’s J and LR+ at the cut-offs ≤ 12.3 cm and ≤ 12.9 cm. Which would you recommend for community screening, and why does J not settle the question?
questions.answer: ≤ 12.3 cm: Se 0.7, Sp 0.9. J = 0.7 + 0.9 − 1 = 0.6; LR+ = 0.7/(1 − 0.9) = 7.0. ≤ 12.9 cm: Se 0.9, Sp 0.7. J = 0.9 + 0.7 − 1 = 0.6; LR+ = 0.9/0.3 = 3.0 (LR− = 0.1/0.7 = 0.14). J is identical, because J counts a missed case and a false alarm as equally bad. In community screening for SAM, a missed child may die while a false positive costs one referral visit, so ≤ 12.9 cm (higher sensitivity) is preferable. The choice rests on the costs of the two errors and on the referral capacity, not on J.

blocks.html: Clinical Prediction Models – Discrimination, Calibration, Validation

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A clinical prediction model combines several predictors to estimate each person’s probability of an outcome, now (diagnostic) or in future (prognostic). Its performance has two parts. Discrimination is how well it ranks people with the outcome above people without it, measured by the c-statistic, the AUC of §15.5.1 applied to the model’s predicted probabilities. Calibration is whether the predicted probabilities are numerically right: among households given 30%, about 30% should have the outcome. Validation estimates how both will hold up in people not used to build the model.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A regression model built to explain (is distance associated with membership, adjusting for confounders?) is judged by its coefficients. A model built to predict (which households are likely to join?) is judged by its predictions (recall §15.1.5, where the two aims lead to different modelling strategies). The same CBHI logistic model of §13.3 can be read both ways. Here it is read as a predictor.

Every performance measure computed on the data used to fit the model is too optimistic. The model has partly fitted the noise of that sample, so it looks better there than it will in new households. Internal validation estimates this optimism by refitting the model in bootstrap resamples (recall §7.2.4). External validation tests the model in new data: another district, or a later year.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Calibration-in-the-large on the development data is perfect by construction. The log-likelihood of a logistic model (recall §13.2.3) is Σ[yᵢ ln pᵢ + (1 − yᵢ) ln(1 − pᵢ)]. Its derivative with respect to the intercept (its slope as the intercept changes; the calculus is beyond this book) is Σ(yᵢ − pᵢ). At the maximum this is zero, so Σpᵢ = Σyᵢ: the mean predicted probability equals the observed proportion. The same argument makes the calibration slope exactly 1 on the development data. Both checks become informative only in new data, or after bootstrap correction.

Calibration slope and intercept. Refit the outcome on the model’s linear predictor (its log-odds): logit(P(y = 1)) = a + b × LP. The slope b shows the spread of the predictions. b < 1 means the predictions are too extreme, too high for high-risk and too low for low-risk people, the signature of overfitting. The intercept a, with b fixed at 1, is calibration-in-the-large: a < 0 means the model overestimates risk on average (Van Calster et al., 2019).

Bootstrap optimism. (1) Fit the model to a bootstrap resample and measure its performance there (training). (2) Measure the same fitted model on the original data (test). (3) Optimism = training − test. (4) Average over 200 or more resamples and subtract the average from the apparent performance (Steyerberg et al., 2001).

Hosmer–Lemeshow (HL) test. Sort people by predicted probability, split them into g groups (usually tenths), and compare observed events O with expected events E (the sum of predicted probabilities) in each group of size n:

HL = Σ (O − E)² ÷ [E(1 − E/n)], referred to χ² with g − 2 degrees of freedom.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The CBHI model of §13.3 predicts membership from distance, wealth and maternal education in 500 households (150 members). Its c-statistic is 0.72: a randomly chosen member has a higher predicted probability than a randomly chosen non-member in 72% of the 150 × 350 = 52,500 member–non-member pairs. The mean predicted probability is 0.39 among members and 0.26 among non-members (recall §13.3). Over all 500 households it is 0.30, exactly the observed 30%, as the Derivation requires.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Sort the 500 households by predicted probability and cut them into ten groups of 50.

    Tenth Mean predicted Expected members E Observed members O
    1 0.10 4.8 5
    2 0.14 6.8 9
    3 0.17 8.4 6
    4 0.20 10.1 6
    5 0.24 12.2 16
    6 0.29 14.3 16
    7 0.34 17.1 18
    8 0.40 20.0 21
    9 0.49 24.5 20
    10 0.64 31.8 33

  2. Largest term, tenth 4: (6 − 10.15)² ÷ [10.15 × (1 − 10.15/50)] = 17.2 ÷ 8.09 = 2.13. The ten terms sum to HL = 7.57 on 10 − 2 = 8 df, p = 0.48.

  3. The expected column sums to 150, the observed number of members (Derivation).

  4. Bootstrap validation (200 resamples, a computer task; the optional In R box shows it): the apparent c-statistic 0.716 has an optimism of 0.010, so the corrected c-statistic is 0.706. The corrected calibration slope is 0.96: new households would get predictions about 4% too extreme on the log-odds scale. With 150 events and 4 coefficients the optimism is small, as expected (recall §13.2.4 on events per variable).

blocks.alt: Calibration plot of the CBHI model
blocks.caption: Figure 15.8. Calibration of the CBHI membership model. Points: observed proportion of members against mean predicted probability in each tenth of predicted risk (step 1). Orange line: smoothed calibration curve corrected for optimism by 200 bootstrap resamples. The dashed diagonal is perfect calibration.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(rms)
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
cb$maternal_education <- factor(cb$maternal_education,
  levels = c("none", "primary", "secondary+"))
f <- lrm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km + wealth_index +
           maternal_education,
         data = cb, x = TRUE, y = TRUE)
round(f$stats[c("C", "Dxy", "Brier")], 3)
set.seed(2026)
round(validate(f, B = 200)[c("Dxy", "Intercept", "Slope"), 1:5], 3)
plot(calibrate(f, B = 200))        # the calibration plot
    C   Dxy Brier 
0.716 0.432 0.184 
          index.orig training   test optimism index.corrected
Dxy            0.432    0.444  0.424    0.020           0.412
Intercept      0.000    0.000 -0.013    0.013          -0.013
Slope          1.000    1.000  0.960    0.040           0.960

C is the c-statistic, 0.716. rms reports discrimination as Somers’ Dxy = 2(C − 0.5), so C = 0.5 + Dxy/2. The validate rows follow the four bootstrap steps: training is the average performance in the resamples, test the average on the original data, and optimism their difference. Corrected Dxy 0.412 gives C = 0.5 + 0.412/2 = 0.706 (step 4). The apparent intercept 0 and slope 1 are the “by construction” values of the Derivation; the corrected slope is 0.96. Brier is the mean squared difference between predicted probability and outcome (0 is perfect).

points.html: Discrimination and calibration are separate. Multiplying every predicted odds by 2 leaves the ranking, and so the c-statistic, unchanged but ruins calibration. Report both.

The HL test is weak evidence either way. It depends on an arbitrary grouping, has low power in small samples, and says nothing about how the model is miscalibrated. Van Calster et al. (2019) “recommend against” it; prefer a calibration plot with slope and intercept. In very large samples a trivial miscalibration becomes significant: in simulations with 50,000 patients and a 0.4% deviation, the HL test was significant in all models (Kramer & Zimmerman, 2007). Here p = 0.48 means “no evidence of miscalibration in 500 households”, not “well calibrated”.

Apparent performance is optimistic. Bootstrap internal validation gives “stable estimates with low bias”; splitting the sample into development and test halves is inefficient (Steyerberg et al., 2001).

External validation is the real test. A model built in one district may be miscalibrated in another where membership is commoner (calibration-in-the-large) or the predictors act differently (slope). Recalibrating the intercept and slope is often enough to update it.

Reporting. TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al., 2024) is the 27-item checklist for studies that develop or validate prediction models, whether by regression or machine learning. It supersedes TRIPOD 2015 (22 items; Collins et al., 2015).
Sample size for prediction models is set by the number of events, the number of predictor parameters and the outcome prevalence, not by a fixed events-per-variable rule (recall §13.2.4).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.9

questions.prompt: Two logistic prediction models for 1-year TB treatment default both have a c-statistic of 0.78 in a validation sample. Model A’s calibration slope is 1.02 and intercept 0.01; model B’s slope is 1.0 but it predicts every patient’s risk about twice too high. What does the shared c-statistic tell you, and what does it fail to tell you? Which model would you give to a counsellor who quotes risks to patients?
questions.answer: The c-statistic measures discrimination: in 78% of defaulter–non-defaulter pairs, both models give the defaulter the higher predicted risk. Both rank patients equally well. It says nothing about calibration, whether the predicted probabilities are numerically right. Model B would tell a patient with a true 10% risk that the risk is about 20%. For ranking patients to target extra support, either would do; for quoting risks, use model A (slope ≈ 1 and intercept ≈ 0 mean its probabilities match observed frequencies), or recalibrate B’s intercept first.

questions.prompt: A model’s apparent Somers’ Dxy is 0.60. Bootstrap validation gives an average optimism of 0.06 in Dxy and a corrected calibration slope of 0.85. Compute the apparent and corrected c-statistics, and explain what a slope of 0.85 says about the predictions.
questions.answer: C = 0.5 + Dxy/2. Apparent C = 0.5 + 0.60/2 = 0.80. Corrected Dxy = 0.60 − 0.06 = 0.54, so corrected C = 0.5 + 0.54/2 = 0.77. A calibration slope of 0.85 (below 1) means the predictions are too extreme: in new patients, high predicted risks will be too high and low ones too low, a sign of overfitting. The log-odds predictions should be shrunk towards the mean (for example, multiplied by 0.85) before use.

questions.prompt: A team reports “Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.48, so the model is well calibrated” for 500 households. Why is this conclusion too strong? What would you expect the same test to show if the same model, with the same small miscalibration, were checked in 50,000 households?
questions.answer: A non-significant test is absence of evidence, not evidence of good calibration. The HL test has low power in samples of a few hundred, its result depends on the arbitrary grouping into tenths, and it gives no information about how the model is miscalibrated. A calibration plot with slope and intercept is more informative. In 50,000 households the same small miscalibration would very probably be significant: the test’s power rises with n, and in simulations with 50,000 patients a 0.4% deviation made it significant in every model (Kramer & Zimmerman, 2007). Significance there would not mean the model is useless.
